source_text: Et haec quidem de patre et de filio et de spiritu sancto breuiter sint nobis dicta, et strictim posita, et non longa disputatione porrecta. latius enim potuerunt porrigi, et propensiore disputatione produci, quandoquidem ad testimonium, quod ita se habeat fides uera, totum et uetus et nouum testamentum possit adduci. sed quia obluctantes aduersus ueritatem semper haeretici sincerae traditionis et catholicae fidei controuersiam solent trahere, scandalizati in Christum, quod etiam deus et per scripturas asseratur et a nobis hoc esse credatur, merito a nobis (ut omnis a fide nostra auferri possit haeretica calumnia) de eo quod et deus sit Christus sic est disputandum, ut non impediat scripturae ueritatem, sed nec nostram fidem, qua unus deus et per scripturas promitur, et a nobis tenetur et creditur. tam enim illi qui Iesum Christum ipsum deum patrem dicunt, quam etiam illi qui hominem illum tantummodo esse uoluerunt, erroris sui et peruersitatis origines et causas inde rapuerunt, quia cum animaduerterent scriptum esse quod unus sit deus, non aliter putauerunt istam tenere se posse sententiam, nisi aut hominem tantum Christum, aut certe deum patrem putarent esse credendum. sic enim calumnias suas colligere consueuerunt, ut errorem proprium approbare nitantur. et quidem illi qui Iesum Christum patrem dicunt, ista praetendunt: si unus deus, Christus autem deus, pater est Christus, quia unus deus: si non pater sit Christus, dum et deus filius Christus, duo dii contra scripturas introducti esse uideantur. qui autem hominem tantummodo Christum esse contendunt, ex diuerso sic colligunt: si alter pater, alter est filius, pater autem deus, et Christus deus, non ergo unus deus, sed duo dii introducuntur pariter, pater et filius; ac si unus deus, consequenter homo Christus, ut merito pater sit deus unus. re uera quasi inter duos latrones cruci figitur dominus, quo modo fixus aliquando est: et ita excipit haereticorum istorum ex utroque latere sacrilega conuicia. Sed neque scripturae sanctae, neque nos causas illis perditionis et caecitatis afferimus, si qua in medio diuinarum ro litterarum euidenter posita aut uidere nolunt, aut uidere non possunt. nos enim et scimus et legimus et credimus et tenemus unum esse deum, qui fecit caelum pariter ac terram, quoniam nec alterum nouimus aut nosse (cum nullus sit) aliquando poterimus. ego sum, inquit, deus: e non est praeter me iustus et saluans. et alio in loco: ego primus et nouissimus, et praeter me non est deus. quis sicut ego? et: quis mensus est palmo caelum, et terram pugillo? quis suspendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera? et Ezechias: ut sciant omnes quia tu es deus solus. ipse praeterea dominus: quid me interrogas de bono? unus deus bonus. apostolus quoque Paulus: guz solus, inquit, habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem; quem uidit hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. et alio in loco: mediator autem unius non est; deus autem unus est. sed quo modo hoc tenemus et legimus et credimus, sic scripturarum caelestium nullam partem praeterire debemus: quippe cum etiam illa quae in scripturis sunt posita Christi diuinitatis insignia nullo modo debemus recusare, ne scripturarum auctoritatem corrumpendo integritatem fidei sanctae corrupisse teneamur. et hoc ergo credamus, siquidem fidelissimum, dei filium Iesum Christum dominum et deum nostrum: quoniam zz principio erat uerbum, et uerbum erat apud deum, et deus erat uerbum. hoc erat in principio apud deum. et uerbum caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis. et: dominus meus et deus meus. et: quorum patres, et ex quibus Christus secundum carnem, qui est super omnia deus benedictus in saecula. Quid ergo dicemus? numquid duos deos scriptura proponit? quomodo ergo dicit, quia deus unus est? aut numquid non et Christus deus est? quomodo ergo, dominus meus et deus meus, Christo dictum est? totum igitur hoc nisi cum propria ueneratione et legitima disputatione teneamus, merito scandalum haereticis praebuisse credemur, non utique ex scripturarum caelestium uitio, quae numquam fallunt, sed humani erroris praesumptione, qua haeretici esse uoluerunt. et in primis illud retorquendum in istos qui duorum nobis deorum controuersiam facere praesumunt. scriptum est, quod negare non possunt, quoniam unus est dominus. de Christo ergo quid sentiunt? dominum esse, aut illum omnino non esse? sed dominum illum omnino non dubitant: ergo si uera est illorum ratiocinatio, iam duo sunt domini.. quomodo igitur iam secundum scripturas unus est dominus? et magister unus Christus est dictus; attamen legimus, quod magister sit etiam apostolus Paulus. non ergo iam unus magister: duos enim magistros secundum ista colligimus. quomodo igitur secundum scripturas unus magister Christus? unus in scripturis bonus dictus est deus; sed iisdem in scripturis bonus etiam Christus positus est. non igitur, si recte colligunt, unus bonus, sed etiam duo boni. quomodo igitur secundum scripturarum fidem unus bonus esse refertur? ac si non putant aliqua ratione offici posse ei quod unus dominus est, per illud quod est dominus et Christus; neque ei quod unus est magister, per illud quod est magister et Paulus; aut illi quod unus est bonus, per illud quod bonus sit nuncupatus et Christus; eadem ratione intellegant offici non posse ab illo quod unus est deus, ei quod deus pronuntiatus est et Christus.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed these things about the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit have been briefly said by us, and briefly stated, and not extended by a long disputation. For they could have been extended more widely, and produced by a more eager disputation, since the whole Old and New Testament can be adduced as testimony that the true faith is so. But because those who oppose the truth, heretics, always draw out a controversy against the sincere tradition and the Catholic faith, scandalized in Christ, because He is also God and is asserted through the Scriptures and is believed by us to be so, it is right that we dispute about this, that Christ is God, in such a way that it does not hinder the truth of Scripture, but also not our faith, by which one God is promised through the Scriptures and is held and believed by us. For both those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father Himself, and those who wanted Him to be only a man, have taken the origins and causes of their error from this, because when they noticed that it is written that there is one God, they did not think that they could hold this opinion in any other way, unless they thought that Christ is either only a man or certainly the Father is to be believed to be God. Thus they are accustomed to collect their calumnies, so that they may strive to approve their own error. And indeed, those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father, put forward this: if there is one God, and Christ is God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; if Christ is not the Father, then, since Christ is the Son of God, two Gods seem to be introduced against the Scriptures. But those who contend that Christ is only a man, collect their arguments in the opposite way: if the Father is another, and the Son is another, and the Father is God, and Christ is God, then two Gods are introduced, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, then consequently Christ is a man, so that the Father may rightly be the one God. In truth, just as the Lord is crucified between two thieves, so He receives the sacrilegious insults of these heretics from both sides. But we do not bring forth the causes of their perdition and blindness, either from the Holy Scriptures or from ourselves, if they do not want to see, or cannot see, the things that are clearly placed in the middle of the divine letters. For we know, and read, and believe, and hold that there is one God, who made heaven and earth, since we do not know, nor can we ever know, another. 'I am', He says, 'God, and there is no just and saving one besides Me.' And in another place: 'I am the first and the last, and there is no God besides Me.' 'Who is like Me?' And: 'Who has measured the heaven with a span, and the earth with a fist?' 'Who has hung the mountains in a balance, and the woods in a scale?' And Ezechias: 'so that all may know that You are the only God.' The Lord Himself also says: 'Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is one good God.' The Apostle Paul also says: 'He alone has immortality, and He dwells in inaccessible light; whom no man has seen, nor can see.' And in another place: 'Now a mediator of one is not; but God is one.' But just as we hold, and read, and believe this, so we ought not to pass over any part of the heavenly Scriptures: for we ought not to refuse the signs of Christ's divinity that are placed in the Scriptures, lest we be held to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith by corrupting the authority of the Scriptures. And therefore we believe, since it is most faithful, that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is our Lord and God: because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. And the Word became flesh, and dwelled among us. And: 'My Lord and my God.' And: 'of whom are the fathers, and from whom Christ is, according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever.' What therefore shall we say? Does Scripture propose two Gods? How then does it say that there is one God? Or does it not also say that Christ is God? How then was it said to Christ: 'My Lord and my God'? Therefore, unless we hold all this with proper veneration and legitimate disputation, we will be believed to have rightly given a scandal to heretics, not from the fault of the heavenly Scriptures, which never fail, but from the presumption of human error, by which heretics want to exist. And first of all, this is to be retorted against those who presume to make a controversy about two Gods for us. It is written, which they cannot deny, that there is one Lord. What then do they think about Christ? That He is the Lord, or that He is not at all? But they do not doubt that He is the Lord: therefore, if their reasoning is true, then there are already two Lords. How then is there one Lord according to the Scriptures? And Christ is said to be one Master; yet we read that the Apostle Paul is also a Master. Therefore, there is not one Master: for we gather two Masters from these things. How then is there one Master, Christ, according to the Scriptures? One God is said to be good in the Scriptures; but in the same Scriptures, Christ is also said to be good. Therefore, if they reason correctly, there is not one good, but two goods. How then is there one good God according to the faith of the Scriptures? And if they do not think that some office can be attributed to the fact that there is one Lord, through the fact that Christ is Lord; nor to the fact that there is one Master, through the fact that Paul is Master; nor to the fact that there is one good, through the fact that Christ is called good; by the same reason, let them understand that an office cannot be taken away from the fact that there is one God, through the fact that Christ is pronounced to be God.

pass_b_english: We have spoken briefly about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, keeping our statement concise and avoiding lengthy debate, though we could have expanded far more and argued at greater length because the entire Old and New Testament bears witness that the true faith stands exactly as we hold it. Yet since heretics who fight against the truth habitually drag the sincere tradition and the catholic faith into controversy, scandalized that Christ is also God and is both proclaimed in Scripture and believed by us to be so, we must dispute that Christ is God in a way that neither impedes the truth of Scripture nor our own faith, by which the one God is promised in Scripture and is held and believed by us. Both those who claim that Jesus Christ is the Father himself and those who insist that he is only a man have drawn the roots and causes of their error from this same point: when they observed that Scripture says there is one God, they concluded they could preserve that conviction only by deciding that Christ must be either a mere man or actually God the Father. That is how they habitually gather their slanders, striving to validate their own error. Those who call Jesus Christ the Father argue like this: if there is one God and Christ is God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; but if Christ is not the Father, then since Christ is the Son of God, two Gods appear to be introduced contrary to Scripture. Those who contend that Christ is only a man argue from the opposite direction: if the Father is one and the Son another, and the Father is God and Christ is God, then two Gods are introduced, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, then Christ must be a man, so that the Father may rightly be the one God. In truth, the Lord is crucified between these two thieves just as he was once fixed on the cross, and so he receives the sacrilegious insults of these heretics from both sides. Yet neither the holy Scriptures nor we ourselves supply the causes of their perdition and blindness if they either refuse to see or cannot see the truths plainly set in the midst of the divine letters. We know, read, believe, and hold that there is one God who made heaven and earth alike, because we know no other and never will. 'I am,' he says, 'God, and there is no just and saving one besides me' (Isaiah 44:6). Again: 'I am the first and the last, and there is no God besides me' (Isaiah 44:6). 'Who is like me?' (Isaiah 44:7). 'Who has measured heaven with a span and the earth with a fist? Who has weighed the mountains in a balance and the hills in scales?' (Isaiah 40:12). And Hezekiah prayed: 'that all may know that you alone are God' (Isaiah 37:16, 20). The Lord himself says: 'Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good' (Matthew 19:17). The apostle Paul also says: 'He alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see' (1 Timothy 6:16). And elsewhere: 'A mediator implies more than one party, but God is one' (Galatians 3:20). But just as we hold, read, and believe this, so we must not pass over any part of the heavenly Scriptures, for we must not refuse the marks of Christ's divinity placed there, lest by corrupting the authority of Scripture we be found to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith. Therefore we believe, because it is most faithful, that Jesus Christ the Son of God is our Lord and God: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). He was in the beginning with God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). And Thomas cried, 'My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28). And again: 'From whom are the patriarchs, and from whom, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever' (Romans 9:5). What then shall we say? Does Scripture propose two Gods? How then does it say there is one God? Or does it not also say that Christ is God? How then was it said to Christ, 'My Lord and my God'? Unless we hold all this with proper reverence and sound reasoning, we will rightly be thought to have given a scandal to heretics, not from any fault in the heavenly Scriptures, which never fail, but from the presumption of human error by which heretics choose to be heretics. First, this must be thrown back at those who presume to manufacture a controversy about two Gods for us. It is written, and they cannot deny it, that there is one Lord (Deuteronomy 6:4; 1 Corinthians 8:6). What then do they think of Christ? That he is the Lord, or that he is not the Lord at all? But they do not doubt that he is the Lord; therefore, if their reasoning is true, there are already two Lords. How then is there one Lord according to Scripture? Christ is called the one Teacher; yet we read that the apostle Paul is also a teacher (1 Timothy 2:7; 2 Timothy 1:11). So there is not one Teacher; by their logic we count two. How then is Christ the one Teacher according to Scripture? One God is called good in Scripture; but in the same Scriptures Christ is also called good (Mark 10:18). So if they reason correctly, there is not one good but two. How then is one good God affirmed according to the faith of Scripture? If they do not think that the fact there is one Lord can be reconciled with Christ being Lord; nor that the fact there is one Teacher can be reconciled with Paul being a teacher; nor that the fact there is one Good can be reconciled with Christ being called good; then by the same reasoning let them understand that the fact there is one God cannot be invalidated by the fact that Christ is declared to be God.

review.notes: All clauses in the Latin source were checked against Pass A and Pass B. Scripture citations added in Pass B (e.g., Isaiah 44:6, John 1:1, etc.) correctly identify the quoted or alluded text. The translation preserves the logical structure of the heretical arguments and the author's refutations. The title 'The Trinity and Heresy' accurately reflects the content of the chapter.
